Travel-time matrices

Source: vignettes/articles/travel-time-matrices.Rmd
travel-time-matrices.Rmd

travel_time_matrix() returns, for every origin and destination, how long the trip takes. This article explains what decides that number, mode by mode, and which arguments change it. All the code runs on the sample network bundled with the package:

library(peabiru)
data_path <- system.file("extdata/spo", package = "peabiru")
network <- build_network(data_path, n_threads = 2)
points <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "spo_points.csv"))
departure <- as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")

Streets: walking, cycling, driving

Each point is first linked to the street network: to the nearest street that the mode may use, looking within 300 m and then within 1600 m. A point with no such street is not routed, and its pairs are missing from the result. The stretch between the point and the street is walked, whatever the mode.

The search then runs over the streets until the time limit: max_trip_duration, or the mode’s own limit (max_walk_time, max_bike_time, max_car_time) when it is lower. Times are rounded down to whole minutes, and pairs beyond the limit are left out of the result rather than returned as NA.

walk <- travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = "WALK",
                           n_threads = 2)
nrow(walk) == nrow(points)^2
#> [1] TRUE

walk15 <- travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = "WALK",
                             max_walk_time = 15, n_threads = 2)
nrow(walk15)
#> [1] 234
range(walk15$travel_time_p50)
#> [1]  0 15

Cyclists ride at bike_speed on streets whose level of traffic stress (LTS, from 1 to 4, derived from the OpenStreetMap tags) is at most max_lts. On more stressful streets they get off and walk the bike, so a cautious cyclist is slower:

lts <- sapply(1:4, function(l) {
  m <- travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = "BICYCLE",
                          max_lts = l, n_threads = 2)
  mean(m$travel_time_p50)
})
setNames(round(lts, 2), paste0("max_lts = ", 1:4))
#> max_lts = 1 max_lts = 2 max_lts = 3 max_lts = 4 
#>       12.52       11.82       10.80        8.17

Cars use each street’s speed (its maxspeed tag, or a default for its road class), pay 10 s for a right turn, 30 s for a left turn and 90 s for a U-turn, and obey turn restrictions.

Public transport

With mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT") a trip is a walk to a stop, up to max_rides vehicles with walking transfers between them, and a walk to the destination, or simply a walk all the way. The search is repeated for every minute of time_window starting at departure_datetime; the matrix reports percentiles of those travel times.

ttm <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure,
  time_window = 10,
  percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 42,
  n_threads = 2
)
head(ttm)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   from_id         to_id          travel_time_p10 travel_time_p50 travel_time_p90
#>   <chr>           <chr>                    <int>           <int>           <int>
#> 1 89a8100c00fffff 89a8100c00fff…               0               0               0
#> 2 89a8100c00fffff 89a8100c007ff…               7               7               7
#> 3 89a8100c00fffff 89a8100c077ff…              10              10              10
#> 4 89a8100c00fffff 89a8100c03bff…               8               8               8
#> 5 89a8100c00fffff 89a8100c033ff…              13              13              13
#> 6 89a8100c00fffff 89a8100c0afff…              23              23              23

Frequency-based feeds and seed

When a feed gives frequencies (a bus every 10 minutes) instead of timetables, the exact departure times are unknown. Each departure minute is then simulated draws_per_minute times with random offsets, so the percentiles also reflect the uncertainty of the schedule. The draws come from a random number generator seeded by seed and the origin’s coordinates: with a seed the result is reproducible; without one it changes from run to run.

again <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 42, n_threads = 2
)
identical(ttm, again)
#> [1] TRUE

other <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 7, n_threads = 2
)
mean(other$travel_time_p50 != ttm$travel_time_p50)
#> [1] 0.09876543

The time window

A single departure minute still varies with a frequency-based feed (the draws), but a wider window also averages over when you leave:

spread <- function(m) mean(m$travel_time_p90 - m$travel_time_p10)
tw1 <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, time_window = 1,
  percentiles = c(10, 50, 90), seed = 42, n_threads = 2
)
c(time_window_1 = spread(tw1), time_window_10 = spread(ttm))
#>  time_window_1 time_window_10 
#>      0.8737997      1.1385460

Walking limits

max_walk_time limits each walk (the access walk, each transfer and the egress walk) and also the walk-only option; transfers are never longer than 1 km. Pairs that need more walking than allowed disappear from the result:

short_walks <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, max_walk_time = 5,
  seed = 42, n_threads = 2
)
c(default = nrow(ttm), max_walk_time_5 = nrow(short_walks))
#>         default max_walk_time_5 
#>             729             270

Threads

n_threads (all cores by default) spreads the origins over threads. The result does not depend on it.

one <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 42, n_threads = 1
)
identical(one, ttm)
#> [1] TRUE

Stopping a long call

An interrupt (Esc, or Ctrl-C in a terminal) stops any of the routing functions within a few tenths of a second and returns to the prompt, with no partial result. setTimeLimit() works too, and tryCatch(interrupt = ) sees the interrupt as it would for R code. build_network() cannot be interrupted.
